\chapter{Sons, Daughters, and Everyone Else}
\label{ch:hi-sons-daughters}
\hlchaptermodality{44}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name four more family and people words in this language.}

Complete HI-C44-people and say all four words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[beṭā]{\hi{बेटा} (beṭā) — son}

\label{lesson:HI-C44-son}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{likhnā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बेटा}}
\textbf{\hi{बेटा}} (\emph{beṭā}) — \textquotedblleft{}son\textquotedblright{}.

The everyday word, not the Sanskrit \emph{putra} that formal Hindi holds in reserve. Its \emph{-ā} is the masculine ending you already met on \hi{बच्चा}. Where the word itself came from is genuinely unsettled: comparative dictionaries reconstruct a Middle Indo-Aryan child-word behind it, with cousins in Punjabi, Gujarati and Marathi, and no agreed Sanskrit source.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of four words for the people around you. Three follow, and each reuses the ones before.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{beṭā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{likhnā}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{बेटा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}son\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[beṭī]{\hi{बेटी} (beṭī) — daughter}

\label{lesson:HI-C44-daughter}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{beṭā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बेटी}}
\textbf{\hi{बेटी}} (\emph{beṭī}) — \textquotedblleft{}daughter\textquotedblright{}.

The same stem, with \emph{-ī} in place of \emph{-ā} — exactly the swap that turns \hi{बच्चा} into \hi{बच्ची}. A great deal of Hindi gender lives in that one final vowel, and this pair is the cleanest example you have met so far: nothing else in the word moves.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of four, and one vowel doing all the work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{beṭī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{beṭā}, and hear only the last vowel move
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{बेटी} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}daughter\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[parivār]{\hi{परिवार} (parivār) — family}

\label{lesson:HI-C44-family}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{beṭī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{परिवार}}
\textbf{\hi{परिवार}} (\emph{parivār}) — \textquotedblleft{}family\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit, and it comes apart in the hand: \emph{pari-}, 'around', on the root \emph{vṛ}, 'to cover, to enclose'. Your family, in this word, is what surrounds you. The same root gives \hi{आवरण} (\emph{āvaraṇ}), 'a covering' — one root, two very different everyday words.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of four, and a word you can take apart rather than memorise.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{parivār}
  \item it once more, slowly, hearing \emph{pari-} at the front
  \item it after \emph{beṭī}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{परिवार} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}family\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[log]{\hi{लोग} (log) — people}

\label{lesson:HI-C44-people}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{parivār} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{लोग}}
\textbf{\hi{लोग}} (\emph{log}) — \textquotedblleft{}people\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{लोक} (\emph{loka}), 'world, realm': the word for the world slid across to mean the people in it. Latin \emph{lucus}, a clearing in a forest, and \emph{lux}, 'light', grow from the same ancient root — an open, lit space first, then whoever stands in it. Hindi hears \hi{लोग} as already plural, so it needs no further ending.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
That closes the run: son, daughter, family, and everyone else.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{log}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{parivār}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{लोग} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}people\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
